title: PteronautOS
essence_lead: PteronautOS is built on ExpressLRS, transformed into a flight controller for ornithopters.
essence_body: Not a quad — no motors, no ESCs, no Betaflight. Movement is generated by waveforms driving two wing servos and a crest rudder servo.
essence_highlight: CRSF (radio) → rx_main → Ornithopter → waveform → PWM servos
arch_zephyrus_desc: MPU6050 gyroscope + Mahony AHRS + dual PID
zeph_lead: Cephalic crest rudder stabilization via MPU6050. Mahony AHRS for attitude estimation, dual PID for roll angle and yaw rate correction.
doc_lead: The manual, the gyro notes, and the web UI reference.
doc_c_ferocity_d: Stroke/return asymmetry and dwell — 0 is a pure sine.
doc_c_waveform_d: The wingbeat curve; amplitude comes from deg/s ÷ 2·freq.
doc_c_glide_d: Wing centre offset for gliding flight.
doc_c_flap_d: Centre bias during the flap stroke (−15…+15 deg).
doc_c_rudder_d: Yaw/roll blend that drives the crest rudder.
doc_c_throttle_d: How much throttle couples into ferocity.
doc_c_failsafe_d: Wings return to neutral if the link drops.
doc_wave_p1: Ferocity controls both the character and the timing of a half-stroke. Internally, the WebUI’s 0–100 setting maps to 0–8. Higher downstroke ferocity shortens the downstroke’s share of the cycle; higher return ferocity shortens the return share. The remaining time is transferred to the opposite half—there is no pause at zero.
doc_wave_p2: The per-profile Ferocity Shape control selects the high-ferocity character. At 0% it favours a finite plateau/square shape. At 100% it favours a rounded pyramidal path. Each half still uses its own ferocity, so a low-ferocity half remains elongated and sinusoidal while a high-ferocity half approaches a direct diagonal traversal.
doc_chart_halves: Each half stretched to equal width
doc_chart_aria_cycle: Wing position over the complete beat cycle
doc_read_p: A 7 / 1 combination clearly produces a short pointed downstroke and a long sinusoidal return. Exact and near-maximum values require care: the current duration law uses the amount remaining below ferocity 8. Consequently, 8 / 0 allocates only about 0.125% of the cycle to the downstroke, while even 8 / 6 allocates about 0.5%. Position remains continuous, but the requested speed and acceleration can become physically unreachable.
doc_caution_body: The explorer describes the commanded mathematical waveform, not guaranteed servo motion. Avoid extreme asymmetric settings until amplitude, frequency, linkage geometry, and servo-speed limits have been verified without aerodynamic load.
doc_lock_sync: Sync: Both sliders move together (click to cycle)
doc_metric: Time allocation: down {down}% · up {up}% · peak phase-speed ratio {ratio}×
tut_lead: Practical guides for preparing the hardware, installing the hermetic firmware, and bringing a new PteronautOS airframe to life.
tut_p1: PteronautOS is not a conventional multirotor stack. It translates CRSF control into a coordinated wingbeat for two wing servos and a crest rudder, with Zephyrus stabilization remaining optional and gracefully degradable.
tut_p2: Start with the flashing guide below. Later guides will cover receiver wiring, binding, the first controlled flap, and tuning the waveform through the WebUI. Every procedure keeps the project’s core rules in view: deterministic timing, centred failsafe behaviour, and no blocking work in the flight loop.
tut_card_desc: Build the ESP8285 target, connect the receiver safely, and install the firmware.
flash_lead: Build and install the hermetic firmware using a CYCLONE ELRS 2.4GHz 7CH PWM RX Receiver as the example.
flash_p1: PteronautOS supports other receiver boards too. Sharing an ESP8285 does not make their wiring identical: the exposed GPIOs, channel assignments, programming connections, and PCB revisions can differ. The power and CH2/CH3 wiring below apply to this CYCLONE example; check your board’s pinout and supported hardware configuration before connecting another receiver.
flash_p2: Before connecting power, remove propulsive loads from the wing mechanism and make sure no servo can drive into a hard stop. Flashing is electrical work; the airframe should remain mechanically safe throughout the procedure.
flash_build_p: Clone the repository, install PlatformIO, and run the following command from the repository root. The PlatformIO project is in src; this command builds the dedicated ESP8285 receiver environment used in this example.
flash_connect_p: For this CYCLONE receiver, use the FTDI adapter’s 5 V power output for the receiver supply, not its 3.3 V power output. Its UART connections are on the signal pins of channels 2 and 3 — there is no need to locate separate UART pads.
flash_connect_note: The 5 V setting refers to receiver power. Check your adapter’s documentation: TX/RX must use ESP8285-compatible 3.3 V logic, even when the supply output is 5 V. Do not connect a second power supply at the same time.
flash_boot_p: Hold BOOT (GPIO0), unplug and reconnect the FTDI USB cable, keep BOOT held for about one second, then release it. The flashing script does not perform an automatic reset, so enter the bootloader manually before running it.
flash_write_p1: From the repository root, run the provided flashing script. It locates a working PlatformIO-bundled flashing tool and the built firmware, selects a serial port, and writes the image with the required flash settings.
flash_write_p2: Automatic port selection looks for macOS /dev/cu.* devices. If several serial devices are connected, or you are using a different operating system, explicitly select the receiver adapter’s port. Replace the example below with your actual device path.
flash_write_p3: To check bootloader communication without writing firmware, use the optional check mode. If it fails, repeat the BOOT power cycle before trying again.
flash_verify_p_a: Power-cycle the receiver without holding BOOT. Confirm that its WiFi access point and WebUI become available (SSID:
flash_verify_p_c: ), then load the configuration and verify the target name before reconnecting servos.
flash_verify_continue_rest: for pin maps and revision-specific wiring notes.
hw_lead: The boards PteronautOS runs on, and how to wire them.
hw_spec_servos_v: 3 PWM channels — left wing, right wing, crest rudder
hw_wiring_p: Three servo channels plus the MPU6050 on the I2C bus. The full pin map, I2C wiring, and v1.0/v1.1 revision differences are in the PWMP7 guide.
hw_compat_lead: Any ExpressLRS 2.4 GHz receiver based on ESP8285 + SX1280/SX1281 with PWM outputs — or a CRSF receiver paired with a CRSF→PWM converter — can run PteronautOS. Prices are approximate and vary by region.
hw_weight_note: Stock weight; removing heatshrink, connectors or housing can cut 30–60%.
hw_esp32_note: ESP32-based receivers (ESP32-C3/S3) use a different architecture and are not yet supported.

archart_title: PteronautOS Architecture — Kernels & Data Flow — PteronautOS
archart_lead: How a CRSF datastream becomes wingbeat and tail: module boundaries, the two mixer kernels, and the state machine that keeps the pterosaur alive when the link dies.
mix_lead: From sticks and gyro to µs on the wire: the complete geometry of every mixer PteronautOS can select — wing axes, rudder blends, elevons, trims and clamps.
st_lead: The ideal design of the gyro-to-wingbeat bridge: Ondas breath modulation, stroke-synchronous feed-forward, phase-locked resonance and aeroelastic PID gain scaling — and an honest map of what the current firmware actually wires up.
st_h2_lineage: Lineage: OrniFlight and a simplified Ondas
sk_p1: The servo kernel maps a normalised angle (−1…+1) to a pulse width through a global envelope defined by servoMinUs (default 988) and servoMaxUs (default 2012). This replaced the old compile-time constants so the 0°/180° swing can be matched to any servo without a rebuild. The values are clamped to [500…1490] and [1510…2500] with min < max enforced.
sk_p2: servoTrimUs[] is a per-ServoFunc correction (±300 µs) applied after mixing. It covers the wing pair (indices 1/2), rudder (3) and the back wings (8/9). Use it to zero out a half-tooth horn offset on a single surface — not to fight an airframe imbalance, which belongs in the mixer or the gyro.
sk_p3: Servo speed limits the rate of pulse change per tick, smoothing hard reversals and protecting gearboxes from snap loads. It is a low-pass on the commanded position, so a low value also softens the flap reversal — tune it against the click at the top and bottom of the stroke. Too slow and the wing lags the waveform; too fast and you re-introduce the snap.
sk_note: For the full pulse/trim/speed parameter list and JSON keys, see the servo-kernel note in the firmware and the WebUI reference.
pwr_p1: A single wing servo can pull 1–2 A transiently at reversal; three servos plus the receiver and gyro demand a rail that never sags. Size the BEC for the stall current of all three servos summed, not their idle current. A 5 V / 3 A switching BEC is a safe baseline for most 2–4 g micro servos; larger wings need 5 A or more.
pwr_p2: Prefer a switching (buck) BEC over a linear one: linears burn the voltage drop as heat and collapse under burst load. Match the BEC voltage to the servo rating (5 V for most micro servos, up to 9 V for HV servos) — but keep the receiver on its own 5 V feed if it lacks a wide-input regulator.
pwr_p3: Most ELRS receivers take 4.5–8.4 V (1S–2S) directly and regulate internally. Feed them the raw battery when possible; only step down for the servos. The MPU6050 breakout (GY-521) accepts 5 V and makes its own 3.3 V.
pwr_p4: Tie every ground to a single star point. A floating ground between the RX and the servos is the classic cause of jitter and brown-outs — one shared GND is non-negotiable.
tel_p1: The receiver samples battery voltage on its ADC pin (GPIO17 on the PWMP7) and reports it back over CRSF telemetry. Wire a voltage divider from the main battery to the ADC pad; calibrate the divider ratio in the config so the radio reads the true pack voltage.
tel_p2: RSSI and link quality come from the SX1280 directly and are exposed in the standard ELRS telemetry slots. Use LQ (link quality) rather than raw RSSI for range decisions — it is the more meaningful metric on 2.4 GHz.
tel_p3: The Zephyrus AHRS can stream roll, pitch and yaw rate as custom telemetry so you can tune the gyro in flight or replay a flight later. This is diagnostic telemetry — keep it off the fast path in production builds to avoid flooding the link.
tel_li1: Barometer (BMP280) for altitude hold and glide control.
tel_li2: Airspeed via a differential pressure sensor for auto-glide triggers.
tel_li3: Current sensor for live power consumption and pack endurance.
tel_li4: GPS for position logging and return-to-home experiments.
fs_p1: Failsafe engages when the CRSF link reports a lost connection or the channel data is stale beyond the configured timeout. The radio's own failsafe is not the source of truth — PteronautOS re-imposes its own centred failsafe so the behaviour is identical regardless of radio brand or bind mode.
fs_p2: On trigger, every servo returns to 1500 µs and the waveform output is suppressed. Wings centre, the crest rudder centres. The voiceAileron/Elevator/Throttle/Rudder channel readouts are reset so the WebUI state poll shows the neutral truth.
fs_p3: The design rule is grace in degradation: a failing MPU6050 must not take the aircraft down. Zephyrus disables itself on gyro failure and the Ornithopter mixer keeps flying on pure stick input — the failsafe path and the gyro path are independent, so one fault never cascades into the other.
fs_p4: Recovery is automatic: when valid CRSF frames resume, the mixer re-engages on the next tick and the servos follow the live channels again. There is no manual reset and no latching — the transition is a single soft ramp back to commanded positions.
budget_p1: The 1 MB ESP8285 flash is dominated by the WebUI: the bundled client build is ~160 KB compressed (~16% of flash) after tree-shaking. The float runtime (_scanf_float, _printf_float, _dtoa_r, _strtod_l …) is ~9.7 KB — real but not the biggest lever. Current baseline sits at ~68.6% flash; the 60% target needs a ~83 KB cut, and the WebUI is the only lever large enough to reach it.
budget_p2: The ESP8285 exposes roughly 23 KB of heap. Config saves must never allocate a big JSON document on the heap — the ornithopter config saver streams directly to LittleFS to avoid exhausting the heap and rebooting mid-poll. Keep DynamicJsonDocument out of the hot path; prefer stack buffers and direct writes.
budget_p3: The manifest forbids exceeding 60% flash / 65% RAM to leave margin for expansion. Measure after every feature; a green build is not a live build until it is flashed and its boot log read.
budget_li1: Tree-shake unused ELRS-RX pages from the WebUI bundle.
budget_li2: Avoid String concatenation in loops — it fragments the heap.
budget_li3: Stream JSON to LittleFS with File::print instead of building documents.
budget_li4: Keep float formatting out of the telemetry hot path (pre-scaled integers).
budget_li5: Prefer #ifdef-gated modules (Zephyrus compiles to no-ops when absent).
first_p1: Power the receiver with the radio bound but sticks neutral. Every servo must sit at 1500 µs. If a horn is not perpendicular to the linkage, unscrew it and re-seat it on the closest spline — never force the neutral with sub-trim on the radio; the flight controller already assumes a true 1500 µs centre.
first_p2: The wing pair is the critical one: both wings must be at the same geometric angle at neutral. A half-tooth difference between left and right is visible as a roll bias in flight and cannot be trimmed away by the gyro without eating into its authority.
first_p3: If a surface moves the wrong way, reverse it in the flight controller config (the servo kernel direction flags), not by flipping the servo or using a radio channel reverse that shifts the 988–2012 µs map. Keep the radio output symmetric around 1500 µs.
first_p4: The servo kernel defaults to servoMinUs 988 and servoMaxUs 2012. Set mechanical endpoints so the wing sweeps its full travel without binding at the extremes. Listen for the buzz of a stalled servo — back off the endpoint until it stops. Endpoints live in the servo kernel, not in the radio: leave the radio at ±100%.
first_p5: Hand-launch into a gentle glide first, motor/flap off, to confirm trim and balance. Only when it glides straight should you engage a low flap frequency and low ferocity. Increase frequency slowly; resonance and aeroelastic effects change with airspeed, so re-trim after each change. Land early on the first battery — the goal is data, not duration.
first_td_roll_v: Right wing tips up, left wing tips down
first_td_pitch_v: Both wings tilt to raise the nose (or elevon equivalent)
first_li1: Wings centred at neutral, both directions correct.
first_li2: Endpoints set with no stall buzz.
first_li3: Failsafe verified — transmitter off — wings and rudder centre.
first_li4: Gyro responds in the correct sense (roll the airframe, rudder should oppose).
first_li5: Battery voltage matches the BEC rating; servos do not brown-out on a full sweep.
zwire_p1: The default Zephyrus I2C pins are GPIO4 (SDA) and GPIO5 (SCL). On the PWMP7 v1.0 those are fine; on v1.1 GPIO2/GPIO5 are not broken out, so Zephyrus uses GPIO1 (SDA, CH2) and GPIO3 (SCL, CH3). Always check the silkscreen against the pin map — GPIO4 is hard-reserved for the SX1280 radio interrupt and must never be repurposed.
zwire_p2: The GY-521 carries its own 4.7 kΩ pull-ups and an AMS1117-3.3V regulator: feed it 5V, it makes its own 3.3V and the logic levels auto-match. Four wires total, no trace cutting, no extra regulator.
zwire_p3: The Mahony AHRS self-calibrates the gyro bias at boot — keep the airframe still for the first second after power-up. Verify the sensor is alive via the serial log: pitch/roll should track the airframe when you tilt it, and the crest rudder should oppose a manual roll (right roll → rudder corrects left). If the bus hangs at boot, you've landed on a reserved pin — re-check the map and move to the correct CH2/CH3 pair.
tx_p1: Put the receiver in bind mode (power with the bind phrase configured, or use the WebUI / button) and start the Bind action on the radio. The default bind phrase darographix yields a fixed UID; a successful bind is confirmed by a solid link LED and live channel movement in the WebUI state poll.
tx_p2: Map the four controls in that order. PteronautOS reads them in CRSF order, so keep CH1–CH4 in the default AETR layout (or match whatever the mixer expects if you reordered them in the config).
tx_p3: Set the radio output to ±100% (CRSF 172–1811 µs around a 992 µs centre). Do not use extended limits — the servo kernel already maps the full 988–2012 µs pulse envelope and clipping the radio only wastes resolution. Sub-trim must remain zero; neutral is 1500 µs by design.
tx_p4: Start with 100% rates and 0% expo. Flap authority is dominated by waveform amplitude, not stick throw, so aggressive radio rates just make the aircraft twitchy. Once it glides and flaps well, add mild expo (15–25%) for a softer centre, and reduce rates only if the roll response over-commands the wings.
tx_li1: Stick full right — right wing rises, left falls.
tx_li2: Stick full back (pitch up) — both wings raise the nose.
tx_li3: Throttle up — flap frequency increases; down — decreases or glide.
wave_p1_a: Explore the parameters live with the
wave_p1_b: before touching the firmware — the same model drives the mixer.
wave_p2: Ferocity is the stroke/return asymmetry. At 0 the wave is a pure sine — equal time up and down. Raising down-ferocity makes the downstroke faster and the upstroke dwell longer (and vice-versa for up-ferocity). This shifts where thrust is produced: a fast downstroke + slow recovery mimics a real bird's power stroke and is the single most effective feel change.
wave_p3: Start at down 8, up 0 for a powerful downstroke, then blend up-ferocity in small steps. Too much asymmetry makes the wings snap at reversal — audible as a click and visible as servo heat.
wave_p4: Amplitude is not set directly; it emerges from frequency and stroke speed. Raising the flap frequency shortens the stroke for a given speed, lowering it lengthens the stroke. The kernel caps amplitude so the servo never leaves the 988–2012 µs envelope. Tune frequency for the airframe's natural flap resonance — a too-high frequency wastes energy, a too-low one drops below effective lift.
wave_p5: The shape mix slider blends the pure sine toward a trapezoid (more dwell at the reversal points). Higher mix = crisper reversals and more thrust at the extremes; lower mix = smoother, more efficient cruise.
wave_p6: Glide angle and flapping angle are both centre offsets (int8, ±15°), not amplitude. Glide sets the common wing angle when the throttle commands glide; flapping shifts the flap stroke's centre. They let you bias the wing for slow flight vs. fast cruise without touching the mechanical linkage.
wave_p7: Begin with Near-sine, confirm stable flight, then move toward Extreme only if you want punch. Every airframe has a different sweet spot — change one parameter at a time.
archart_gb1: maps throttle (armed) to a 1000…2000 µs ESC command (SF_MOTOR), idle when disarmed;
archart_gb2: mixes the tail: V-tail profiles use an elevon blend (aileron+elevator / aileron−elevator), classic profiles use a separate elevator surface;
archart_gb3: lets Zephyrus (when enabled) inject roll and pitch PID corrections into the tail servos, clamped to ±250 µs (ZEPHYR_GEARBOX_CLAMP_US) so a sensor glitch can never stall a servo;
archart_gb4: keeps the same rudder mixer and µs/trim/clamp envelope as the waveform kernel.
archart_li1: Channels are normalized early. Every raw value in the 172–1811 CRSF window is mapped to −1…+1 (_crsfToNorm) or to a percentage once, and only that unit flows through the mixers — no repeated magic constants.
archart_li10: Geometry & output. The shaped −1…+1 wave is scaled into degrees, mixed against aileron/elevator steering (±60° authority × scale), offset by the glide/flap-centre trim, clamped 0…180°, then converted to µs through the configurable servoMinUs…servoMaxUs envelope (988…2012 defaults) with per-function trim.
archart_li11: Glide branch. Below the flap threshold the oscillator decays, and the wings hold a static glide angle — an ideal bench-and-launch state.
archart_li2a: Outputs are tagged, not pinned. The mixers write into _f[ServoFunc]. Which physical PWM output a tag drives is decided later by the profile's funcMap — see the
archart_li2b: .Re-pinning a model never touches mixer math.
archart_li3: The kernel is a compile-time family, a runtime choice. Both the waveform flapper and the gearbox controller live in the binary; the active profile picks the kernel every update tick.
archart_li4: Failsafe is not an event, it is a state. Link-down, bench mode and stick-override are explicit gates in update(), so servos can never run away while the radio is silent.
archart_li5: Flap gate with hysteresis. Throttle must cross the flap threshold (default raw ≈303, ≈1.08 ms PWM-equivalent) to enter flapping; it leaves only below threshold − 50 hysteresis, so marginal throttle never chatters the wings.
archart_li6: Frequency. A FlappingOscillator advances with real elapsed time (µs clock, dt capped at 100 ms). The cadence target blends the CH6 flap-frequency channel and throttle via the profile's throttleFrequencyMix, within 0.5 Hz…flapBaseFreq/10.
archart_li7: Amplitude. Throttle percentage of the servo-speed ceiling ampMax = degPerSec / (2·f) (with degPerSec = 60°/servoSpeed_ms), hard-capped at 55° pre-multiplier. Amplitude therefore collapses naturally at high frequency — the wing never demands more than the servo can deliver.
archart_li8: Ferocity. Down-stroke (power) and up-stroke (recovery) ferocities are shaped per stroke, modulated asymmetrically by elevator (pull-up hardens the downstroke, push-over hardens the upstroke) and by throttle coupling, then bounded 0…8 before the shape function.
archart_li9: Yaw differentials. Rudder adds L/R-opposed ferocity (rudderFerocityRange) and L/R-opposed amplitude (rudderAmplitudeDifferential) while the stroke-reversal phase stays shared between the wings — the turn authority comes from asymmetric dwell, not from desynchronised wings.

archart_p1: PteronautOS is an ExpressLRS 4.x fork that replaced the "PWM passthrough" tail of the receiver with a dedicated flight-control layer. The data path is deliberately short:
archart_p11: The next layer down — exactly which waveform shape the numbers produce, and how every profile wires functions to PWM outputs — lives in the
archart_p11b: article, and the servo-timing envelope is documented in the
archart_p2: Four structural ideas keep the beast stable and the code small:
archart_p3: A kernel is the block that turns normalized channels into servo-function µs. PteronautOS has two families, discriminated by the mixer-profile number:
archart_p4: Selection happens in update() with the single test PROFILE_IS_GEARBOX (activeProfile ≥ 3). The profile itself is a runtime value: it starts from the MIXER_PROFILE build flag (legacy ORNITHOPTER_GEARBOX=1 still maps to profile 5) but can be switched live from the WebUI via setOrnithopterProfile() — the firmware re-targets a new airframe without a reflash. There are eight profiles in total; their exact funcMap layouts are tabulated in the Mixer Reference.
archart_p5: The waveform kernel is what most people mean by "PteronautOS": two wing servos run a phase-continuous oscillation whose shape is sculpted every cycle. Its anatomy:
archart_p6: The gearbox kernel trades pure wingbeat for a motorised drivetrain plus conventional tail surfaces. Because a motor turns continuously, this kernel is stateless per tick — no oscillator — and instead:
archart_p7: One ornithopter rig can even carry both personalities: flapping launch with the waveform kernel, cruise on the gearbox — the runtime profile switch is that single line in update().
archart_p8: update() is called on a fixed ~10 ms cadence from the WiFi/servo loop and gates on three flags before any mixer runs:
archart_p9: The centre-on-loss behaviour is duplicated in two layers on purpose: the CRSF stack failsafes the channel data, and the Ornithopter layer failsafes the geometry (including the oscillation state). A dead radio therefore leaves a gliding, controllable airframe — never a flailing one.
archart_st1b: Full kernel output follows the sticks
archart_st2b: Neutral sticks are injected, throttle parked below the flap threshold — glide + trim edits are visible live
archart_st3b: Firmware-injected channel values replace CRSF entirely (servo sweeps, tests)
archart_st4b: All functions centre to 1500 µs, oscillator reset, motor → min; CRSF packet loss also centres at RX level
archart_td_gear_act: Motor ESC, V-tail or elevator + rudder
archart_td_gear_model: Geared / motorised flapper with conventional tail surfaces
archart_td_wave_model: Direct-drive servo ornithopter — the classic PteronautOS
mix_fm_row2: Left wing · Right wing · Back-left wing
mix_gb1: Motor — SF_MOTOR: when armed, throttle 0…1 maps to 1000…2000 µs; disarmed or link-down forces the minimum (motor stopped).
mix_gb2: Rudder — identical equation to the section above.
mix_gb3: Tails — two families. Classic profiles (6/7) drive a separate elevator: µs = 1500 + elevatorNorm·500 + pitchPID + trim. V-tail profiles (3/4/5) elevon-mix both channels onto the two tail servos:
mix_gyro_pitch_wave: — (injected as wave modulation in the Zephyrus layer)
mix_gyro_rudder_gear: gyroRudderCorrection added to the fin rudder µs
mix_gyro_rudder_wave: gyroRudderCorrection added to the crest rudder µs
mix_li1: Ferocity differential (rudderFerocityRange): left gets +ferocity, right −ferocity — the two wings dwell differently but keep a shared reversal phase (limiarShared), so turns are pure roll torque, never desynchronisation.
mix_li2: Amplitude differential (rudderAmplitudeDifferential): left amplitude ×(1+Δ), right ×(1−Δ) — symmetric divergence around the throttle-set stroke.
mix_meaning_backwing: Rear wing pair of a 4-wing airframe (mirror of the front pair, own trim)
mix_meaning_none: Reserved — no function (first PWM slots stay free for BOOT and I2C)
mix_meaning_rudder: Head/crest rudder (waveform) or fin rudder (gearbox) — yaw + roll blend
mix_p10: Defaults: rudderYawWeight = 65%, rudderRollWeight = 35% (runtime-tunable in the WebUI, stored per backup). Roll coupling on the rudder is what lets a wing-heavy pterosaur hold coordinated turns without yaw-string gymnastics; reduce the roll weight if the head rudder feels too aggressive in roll.
mix_p11: The gearbox kernel runs statelessly every tick. Its three sub-mixers:
mix_p12: On the gearbox kernel, Zephyrus injects both roll and pitch PID corrections into the tail servos (roll anti-phase, pitch common-mode), each hard-clamped to ±250 µs (ZEPHYR_GEARBOX_CLAMP_US). A gyro glitch can therefore waggle, but never stall, a tail servo.
mix_p13: Three different injection points exist depending on kernel and axis:
mix_p14: Trims & limits. Every function has a signed per-servo trim (servoTrimUs[tag], default 0, ±300 µs) added last, and every value passes _clampServo — an absolute 500…2500 µs safety clamp that outranks everything. On failsafe or link-down, all functions return to 1500 µs and a gearbox motor to minimum, so the model always glides to neutral.
mix_p15a: Ready for the practical layer? The
mix_p15b: tutorial shows how these numbers feel from the sticks, and the
mix_p15c: article shows where each mixer sits in the pipeline.
mix_p1a: This page documents the mixer layer of src/lib/Ornithopter/Ornithopter.cpp and the profile system of OrnithopterConfig.h. For the surrounding architecture, start with the
mix_p1b: ; for pulse timing and trim ranges, see the
mix_p3: A runtime profile provides the funcMap: an array that maps PWM output index → ServoFunc. The first three slots (PWM 1…3) are always SF_NONE — they belong to the BOOT strap and the I2C bus — so real servo functions begin at PWM index 3 (the firmware comment spells this out: index 3 = CH4, 4 = CH5, 5 = CH6).
mix_p3_tags_intro: Every output of every mixer is a µs value written into _f[], indexed by a ServoFunc tag. Tags are transport — they say what a signal means, never where it is wired:
mix_p4: Selection: build-time flag MIXER_PROFILE (legacy ORNITHOPTER_GEARBOX=1 → profile 5), then runtime-overridable through the WebUI (setOrnithopterProfile). The kernel test is simply activeProfile ≥ GEARBOX_2VTAIL_1RUD.
mix_p4_intro: Eight mixer profiles exist. Profiles 0–2 drive the waveform kernel (flapping wings), profiles 3–7 the gearbox kernel (motor + tails):
mix_p5: All channel values enter the mixers normalized: _crsfToNorm maps the raw 172…1811 window linearly onto −1…+1. Steering commands are then scaled by the per-profile authority sliders (aileronScale, elevatorScale, 0–100%) times ±60° (ORNI_STEER_MAX_DEG).
mix_p6: Mirror geometry. Wing servos are mirror-mounted, which swaps the meaning of common-mode and differential terms. The code therefore treats aileron (roll) as common — it adds to both wings, which becomes a differential physical deflection — and elevator (pitch) as differential in code, which becomes a common physical deflection. The angle equations, with ORNI_NEUTRAL_ANGLE_DEG = 100° and the 2× multiplier applied to deviation terms only:
mix_p7: degL/degR are the instantaneous stroke deflections of the left and right wing, each the product of its own amplitude and a ferocity-shaped wave. Elevator-up strengthens the downstroke; elevator-down the upstroke (asymmetric ferocity). Yaw splits the wings in two complementary ways:
mix_p8: Angles are clamped 0…180° and converted to pulses with the configurable envelope servoMinUs…servoMaxUs (defaults 988…2012): µs = min + angle·(max−min)/180, plus the per-function trim. The glide/flap centre offsets (glideAngleDeg, flappingAngleDeg, ±15°) enter as static terms on their respective branch — so glide and flap centres can be tuned independently per flight profile.
mix_p9: The rudder mixer is shared verbatim by both kernels — one equation, two airframes:
st_aero1: All Ondas and SSFF modulation is scaled by a coefficient that knows whether the ornithopter is flapping or gliding — aeroelastic gain modulation. In the servo (waveform) kernel the selector is the flapping gate with its 50 µs hysteresis:
st_aero2: In the gearbox kernel the selector is the motor state (armed && throttleNorm > 0.1f). Defaults:
st_aero_flap_when: Wings flapping — or gearbox motor running
st_aero_glide_when: Wings still — glide, or gearbox motor off
st_anchor1: The oscillator's damping is exposed as a tunable anchor. The base law is a damped spring toward the cadence target:
st_anchor2: At anchorGain = 0 (default) damping is tight — rapid convergence to the commanded cadence. Higher values raise k₂ toward 110 at gain 100, locking the rhythm harder and rejecting perturbations. Tuning range 0–100.
st_auth_leg_gear: roll PID → aileron side of elevon mix
st_authority: Scaling to 0–1 makes the 0–100 slider the authority of the gyro over the wing: at 100 the gyro fully owns the modulation, at 0 it is off. Authority by kernel:
st_balance1: The integral term shifts the stroke centre: a persistent nose-up bias strengthens the downstroke, a persistent nose-down bias strengthens the upstroke.
st_balance2: Balance is the most destabilising channel when set high — the ideal tuning guide keeps it low (5–15) and adds it last. Ferocity application, combining pilot command, Ondas and SSFF biases, keeps the pilot's authority over the full [1.0, 8.0] window:
st_bridge_5: Crest rudder µs offset (servo & gearbox kernels)
st_bridge_6: Gearbox: roll PID → V-tail aileron surfaces
st_bridge_7: Gearbox: pitch PID → elevon / elevator surfaces
st_cadence1: A positive pitch error (nose up) advances the oscillator phase, shortening the current half-stroke; a negative error retards it. The ideal law scales the oscillator spring:
st_cadence2: The oscillator advance() consumes it as error = kGain · kGainMod · cadenceTarget − kDamp · cadence. Tuning range 0–100, default 20.
st_ferocity1: The P and D terms are blended into a single ferocity signal that sharpens or softens the waveform's dwell:
st_ferocity2: With ferocityPGain = 0 (the default) the behaviour is D-only — rapid pitch changes produce sharper strokes while steady flight stays sinusoidal.
st_lag: Gearbox PID corrections are clamped to ±250 µs (ZEPHYR_GEARBOX_CLAMP_US) before mixing; the crest-rudder path is clamped to ±200 µs. One frame of lag is inherent: aeroGainScale is computed in the gearbox mixer but consumed by the next zephyrusUpdate() — 4 ms at 250 Hz, negligible for mechanical servos.
st_lineage1a: Ondas is not a PteronautOS invention. The wave-modulation family — breath-pause cadence control, stroke-shape ferocity, asymmetric dwell, and the aeroelastic coupling of wing load to PID authority — lives and evolves in the
st_lineage1b: project, whose wiki and simulator carry the advanced algorithms (including the
st_lineage2: PteronautOS embeds a partially simplified implementation: the same mathematical breath geometry, scaled to an ESP8285 with one MPU6050 and up to nine servos. Where OrniFlight simulates continuous aeroelastics and explores whole envelope families offline, PteronautOS must decide in 4 ms ticks, on an 80 MHz core, with the ExpressLRS radio stack sharing the same silicon. Every gain in this article exists in both projects; the firmware constants below are the airborne subset.
st_nan: All four are guarded by a NaN trap (if any input is NaN, all four are zeroed) so a corrupted I²C frame can never reach the mixer arithmetic. Seven fields on Ornithopter receive the bridge data:
st_ondas: Ondas (Portuguese: "waves") is the three-channel breath system that maps the pitch PID's raw P, I and D terms onto three orthogonal dimensions of the flapping waveform. It is a proprioceptive loop: the gyro's sense of pitch directly shapes the wing motion, and the wing motion changes the pitch the gyro feels.
st_pipeline: The bridge from the gyro to the wingbeat is deliberately short — four files, no dynamic allocation, no queues:
st_resonance1: Resonance is a phase-locked lock-in amplifier: it multiplies the pitch error rate by sin(oscillator phase) and accumulates — reinforcing the stroke exactly when a correction is most effective, damping it when it would fight the wing.
st_resonance2: The accumulated value is injected into both stroke and return ferocity for the next frame. At resonanceGain = 0 (default) the whole path is disabled. The leaky decay prevents runaway accumulation during sustained disturbance.
st_shape: The waveform itself follows the OrniFlight stroke family: each half uses its own ferocity, a shared reversal threshold keeps left/right wings in phase, and a per-profile shape mix continuously transmutes a flat dwell/plateau stroke into a rounded pyramidal path. The interactive explorer below renders the commanded geometry for any down/up ferocity pair — the same curve the mixer requests each tick.
st_ssff1: Stroke-synchronous feed-forward is philosophically different from every PID term: it corrects the next half-stroke from what the gyro measured during the current one. At each zero-crossing of the flapping sine (wing reversal), the mean pitch error rate of the finished half-stroke becomes a bias on the opposite half's ferocity.
st_ssff2: Up-bias is applied to the downstroke (correcting for error accumulated on the preceding upstroke); down-bias to the upstroke. When ssffGain drops to zero the biases are explicitly cleared so a WebUI disable never leaves stale values in the waveform. The accumulator is 32-bit and reset per half-stroke — at 250 Hz it would need ~24 days of continuous flapping to overflow, which is not a practical concern.
st_status_final_c: holds the continuously advanced ONDAS research.
st_status_intro: Honest map, current firmware (Ornithopter.cpp @ 72c63020). The ideal laws above are the design; the code contains the full parameter surface, the constants, the WebUI sliders and the bridge shim — but a flight-test scaffolding block currently disconnects most of the gyro from the servo kernel:
st_status_li1: Cadence, Ferocity-PD, Balance, Resonance, SSFF — all present as parameters and in the bridge, but their consumption sites (kGainMod, ferocitySignal, iBias, resonanceBias) are pinned to zero or reset every frame (Ornithopter.cpp:282–284, 311–313, 354).
st_status_li2: Crest rudder stabilization is zeroed inside the flapping branch, so the rudder correction currently acts only in the glide branch — the opposite of what flight needs (most disturbances arrive mid-flap).
st_status_li3: The gearbox kernel is the live exception. It reads gyroAileronCorrection / gyroElevatorCorrection / gyroRudderCorrection and applies them with clamps (lines 436–451) — the STEP-7 zeroing block lives only in the servo kernel.
st_status_p1: Committed with the i18n work as a "STEP 7" NaN-guard test and never rolled back, this block means today's servo-kernel behaviour is:
st_status_p2: This is not a criticism of the math — it is a known, named state: the stabilization modules are compiled in, parameterized, bridged, and waiting for the STEP-7 scaffolding to be removed and replaced by a real NaN policy (the Validatio guards already give the MPU data a clean path). Until then, treat the Ondas/SSFF/resonance tuning guide above as the flight-ready specification, verified against Zephyrus.cpp:729–737 and OrnithopterWaveform.h, but not yet airborne.
st_terms: The four raw terms are written in Zephyrus::update() immediately after the pitch PID computes its correction:
st_tune_li1: Zero every gain. Fly manual only; the airframe must be stable and predictable before the gyro earns a vote.
st_tune_li2: Enable Zephyrus's crest rudder (roll+yaw PID). Verify the rudder resists a gentle wing-rock before anything touches the waveform.
st_tune_li3: Cadence (P→Phase) from 10 upward. Too high = jerky wings, phase hunting; too low = nothing. Right = wings feel "connected" to pitch.
st_tune_li4: Ferocity D (D→Dwell) from 10. Too high = the waveform oscillates between sharp and soft; right = rapid pitch changes sharpen the stroke, steady flight stays sinusoidal.
st_tune_li5: Ferocity P (optional) from 5 — blends P authority into the dwell.
st_tune_li6: Balance (I→Asymmetry) last, low. This is the most destabilizing channel; 5–15 only. It counters persistent drift, never transient bumps.
st_tune_li7: SSFF from 5, only after cadence and ferocity hold. Too high = over-correction and half-stroke flutter; right = visible damping of pitch oscillation amplitude.
st_tune_li8: Aeroelastic coefficients last. Tune glide first (wings still), then flap. Keep the gyro an authoritative copilot, not a nervous pilot.
st_tuning: The ideal flight-test sequence — each step is a flight, not a slider drag:
st_webui1: The ornithopter panel shows two stabilization groups when the build includes Zephyrus. Ondas & SSFF sliders (0–100): Cadence P→Phase, Ferocity D→Dwell, Ferocity P→Dwell, Balance I→Asymmetry, Anchor k₂, Resonance, SSFF Gain. Aeroelastic group: Glide Coefficient and Flap Coefficient. All values persist through POST /pteronautos/config and stream back through GET /pteronautos/state:
st_webui2: aero_gain_scale is computed and read-only. POST accepts partial updates and clamps every field to [0, 100] server-side.
cc_lead: The symbiosis: PteronautOS is the spirit, YOSHIMITSU is the hand. Two boards, one flight — split across the bridge by one admin command: MUSHIN (無心).
cc_arch_p1: In companion mode the two MCUs stop being a receiver and a converter and become one brain with two halves. This diagram is the eternal map:
cc_h2_gyro: Why the gyro stays on the RP2040
cc_gyro_p1: The MPU6050 is physically wired to the RP2040 — so the PID is computed there too. Shipping raw gyro samples over the bridge to PteronautOS, only to PID them and ship corrections back, would be pure latency devotion. The hand that holds the gyro corrects the stroke: Zephyrus lives on the companion, not on the receiver.
cc_split_p1: Each half computes what it is closest to.
cc_ptero_duty: CRSF RX decode + mixer intent (waveform soul) — what is shortly before
cc_yoshi_duty: gyro + PID (Zephyrus, local) + companion compute + PIO servo-PWM — what is closer to muscle memory
cc_cores_p1: The RP2040-Tiny is the only ELRS-PWM platform with hardware PIO state machines — eight of them — for glitch-free servo PWM. Its two Cortex-M0+ cores split cleanly:
cc_core1_duty: — mixer + flapping offload: the trajectory the hand will trace.
cc_core0_duty: — PIO servo-PWM: the samples that actually move the wing and the crest rudder.
cc_flag_p1: MUSHIN (無心, the no-mind) decides whether YOSHIMITSU stays a silent converter or wakes as the companion hand. It boots armed — the cheatcode; the JIGUANG admin console commands it over USB serial: MUSHIN reports, MUSHIN ON/OFF arms or disarms. The choice persists in flash (EEPROM byte 6 on the RP2040) — configuration by command, not by recompile.
cc_cheat_p1: No other ELRS-PWM board carries a dual-core with hardware PIO. For the price of the tiny board you get two cores — one pure muscle, one companion computer. Elsewhere you would pay more and always be weaker.
cc_cheat_p2: Cheaper, and always stronger: this is the hermetical shinobi's answer to the market.
cc_h2_hermetic: Helicopter or flapping — the same stroke
cc_hermetic_p1: From the sword's view, helicopter or flapping is the same: the mixer emits a canonical trajectory — channel to servo path — and the hand never asks which vehicle it carries. Back-turned — the pose flies on, only the gaze changes.
cct_lead: Give the sword a hand: wire the RP2040-Tiny as the companion core.
cct_parts_3: three servos — wing L/R, crest rudder
cct_parts_4: PteronautOS receiver, flashed with the companion bridge
cct_wire_p1: The MPU6050 connects directly to the RP2040's I2C — SDA and SCL — not to the receiver. The gyro belongs to the hand.
cct_flash_p1: Flash PteronautOS normally, then flash the YOSHIMITSU sketch for the RP2040-Tiny. The companion hand wakes through the MUSHIN command (無心) — one firmware, one scroll.
cct_flag_p1: MUSHIN (無心) boots armed by default — the hand strikes before the thought. Open the USB serial console and type MUSHIN to report, MUSHIN ON/OFF to arm or disarm. No reflash: the choice persists in flash and the flasher bridge in MEDITATION is never touched.
cct_verify_p1: Open the USB console and read the JIGUANG tale: the stance is MEDITATION, the bridge is up, and the gyro reports from the hand — not from the receiver.
tut_card_cc_desc: Wire the RP2040-Tiny as the hand: gyro, PID and PIO servo-PWM on one dual-core.
yos_jiguang_mushin: And the youngest cheatcode of the scroll: MUSHIN (無心) — the muscle-memory mode. PteronautOS plans the wave (the geist), YOSHIMITSU strikes (the hand): servo intents cross the bridge UART as the no-mind protocol v0, the local Zephyrus gyro PID holds the crest, and the PIO PWM answers at the muscle — dual-core, glitchless, a cheatcode no other ELRS-PWM board can wear. JIGUANG administers it from the throne: MUSHIN reports, MUSHIN ON/OFF arms or disarms and persists in flash. In MEDITATION the same two wires carry esptool’s SLIP untouched.
yos_dual_intro_markdown: YOSHIMITSU is the **Hermetic Shinobi** with **six stances** — one soul, not two tools. A single sketch builds for both boards; the stances switch by USB command, a GPIO0 button (ESP32-S3), or RESET-taps (RP2040-Tiny):
yos_stance_kincho_html: CRSF→PWM converter — the parry (CRC discards the false). No channel names, no gyro.
yos_stance_manji_html: Converter + Zephyrus gyro link (optional MPU6050) — the levitation.
yos_stance_flea_html: Power-cycle jig — the lift that drops the RX into its bootloader.
yos_stance_meditation_html: Pocket flasher — the sponge-head, saving energy, ready to be flashed.
yos_stance_nss_html: No-Sword bench — direct servo over USB, no RF.
yos_stance_back_html: The deceptive idle — a living UART mirror. Never looks back.
yos_targets_markdown: One sketch, two targets: `sketches/yoshimitsu/yoshimitsu.ino` compiles for the **Waveshare RP2040-Tiny** (lightest, no onboard button) *and* any native-USB **ESP32-S3**, with the standard arduino-pico / arduino-esp32 cores.
yos_yoshimitsu_markdown: **YOSHIMITSU** is the recommended firmware. It boots in **KINCHO** (the converter) and moves between stances. The USB console is the canonical switch on both boards — `KINCHO` → `MANJI` → `FLEA` → `MEDITATION` → `NSS` → `BACK` → `POSE <n>`. On the ESP32-S3 the BOOT button (GPIO0) is a second surface:
yos_boot_act1_html: cycle KINCHO → MANJI → NSS → BACK → KINCHO →
yos_boot_act3_html: restart the receiver (run the new firmware)
yos_boot_act4_html: FLEA — drop the receiver into its bootloader
yos_harness_markdown: The wiring is **one permanent harness** — the same wires serve every stance, so you never re-wire between flying and flashing. In MEDITATION the USB→UART path is a *pure transparent bridge* (no line parsing), so esptool's binary SLIP traffic passes through untouched. Full source: `sketches/yoshimitsu/yoshimitsu.ino` (the config shell) and `src/Yoshimitsu.h` (the library core).
yos_conv_markdown: **KINCHO** — the converter stance — reads CRSF at 420 000 baud on the UART, drives servos with a 988–2012 µs window mapped from the 172–1811 channel range, and centres them on a 500 ms failsafe. The parry is the CRC check: a corrupt frame is discarded before it ever reaches a servo. The converter is **channel-agnostic** — servos are `SERVO_PIN_1..8` and the `CHANNEL_TO_SERVO` table decides which CRSF channel feeds each; channel *meaning* belongs to the mixer/kernel, never to the board.
yos_conv_li1_html: ESP32-S3: RX TX → GPIO44, RX RX → GPIO43, common GND, shared 5 V rail.
yos_conv_li3_html: Servos: `SERVO_PIN_1..3` (three more on the S3) — overrideable in the PIN MAP block.
yos_manji_markdown: For a **gyro-stabilised ornithopter**, use **MANJI_DRAGONFLY** — the same converter plus the **Zephyrus** link: an optional MPU6050 on `GYRO_SDA`/`GYRO_SCL` feeds a yaw-rate correction into the crest servo. Without a gyro wired, MANJI_DRAGONFLY degrades gracefully into KINCHO. A commercial CRSF→PWM converter board has no gyro path at all — EP2-class receivers carry no IMU, so Zephyrus lives in YOSHIMITSU, not in the receiver.
yos_pwm_markdown: If your receiver already speaks PWM (a 5 ch or 7 ch board), you do not need the converter stances at all — MEDITATION below is then your only reason to own the S3.
yos_flasher_problem_markdown: **The problem:** EP2-class receivers (HappyModel EP2, EP1, EPW6, …) expose CRSF on castellated pads and carry a tiny BOOT pad. Using an FTDI adapter means holding a probe against two 1 mm pads *while* power-cycling the receiver — awkward, and you re-solder or re-clip every time the firmware needs an update.
yos_flasher_solution_markdown: **The solution:** let the ESP32-S3 be the *flasher*. One GPIO holds the receiver's BOOT pad low; a small P-MOSFET switches the receiver's 3.3 V rail under software control; the USB port becomes the serial port. Press one button on the S3 and it performs the exact power-cycle dance that drops an ESP8285 into its ROM bootloader — then esptool writes straight through the bridge. No FTDI, no probes, no repeated soldering: solder the receiver's pads *once* to a short pigtail and reuse it forever.
yos_bridge_note_a_html: The bridge works with every ESP8285/SX1280 ELRS receiver that exposes TX, RX, 3V3, GND and a BOOT pad — the overwhelming majority of the *concrete boards* in the
yos_bridge_note_b_html: . It also flashes the S3 itself, of course: BOOT button + USB is all that needs there.
yos_wiring_markdown: Wire the jig with the S3 unpowered. The MOSFET switches the receiver's 3.3 V rail: source → S3 3V3, drain → EP2 3V3, gate → S3 GPIO10 with a 10 kΩ pull-up to 3V3 (gate high = MOSFET off). GPIO9 drives the BOOT pad.
yos_polarity_body_markdown: ⚠ feed the receiver **3.3 V only**, never 5 V, while it is on the jig. Verify the MOSFET with a voltmeter before connecting a receiver: with GPIO10 HIGH the drain must read 0 V; with GPIO10 LOW it must read 3.3 V.
yos_mode_markdown: MEDITATION boots into *transparent passthrough* (USB ↔ UART at 115 200 baud). To enter **flash mode**, double-tap the S3's BOOT button (or type `FLEA` over the USB serial). The sketch then:
yos_mode_li2_html: switches the MOSFET off for 120 ms (receiver power off),
yos_mode_li3_html: switches it back on and waits 900 ms (receiver powers up inside its bootloader),
yos_mode_li4_html: releases GPIO9 — the RX now sits in the ROM bootloader, waiting for esptool,
yos_mode_li5_html: resumes USB↔UART passthrough so esptool can talk to it.
yos_mode_reset_markdown: Because the bridge cannot drive the classic DTR/RTS auto-reset lines, always flash with `--before no_reset` — the power-cycle dance above *is* the reset. After flashing, a **single** BOOT tap power-cycles the receiver again so it boots the new firmware; a double-tap would merely re-enter flash mode.
yos_esptool_markdown: Build the firmware (or fetch a release), then run esptool against the S3's USB serial port. On macOS the port shows up as `/dev/cu.usbmodem*`:
yos_esptool_code_html:
# 1. Build PteronautOS (from the repository root)
pio run -e PteronautOS_ESP8285_2400_RX

# 2. Drop the RX into flash mode (type FLEA, or double-tap BOOT), then:
python3 -m esptool --chip esp8285 \
  --port /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX --baud 115200 \
  --before no_reset write_flash \
  --flash_mode dout --flash_size 1MB --flash_freq 40m \
  0x0 .pio/build/PteronautOS_ESP8285_2400_RX/firmware.bin

# 3. Restart the RX once more (single BOOT tap) to run the new firmware.
yos_esptool_after_markdown: The flash settings (dout, 1 MB, 40 MHz) match the stock ESP8285 ELRS target — never use qio or a larger size. After flashing, the very same USB port shows the receiver's boot log: open it at 115 200 baud and watch for the PteronautOS banner and, once a transmitter binds, the CRSF link-up messages. The bridge doubles as your field console for live telemetry.
yos_verify_li1_html: FLEA must power-cycle the RX and leave it waiting — the 3.3 V dips for ~120 ms.
yos_verify_li2_html: esptool reports `Chip is ESP8285` and finishes with `Hash of data verified`.
yos_verify_li3_html: The boot log shows the PteronautOS banner and, with the radio on, a link-up message.
yos_verify_li4_html: Wiggle the sticks: servos track smoothly; switch the radio off: wings centre to 1500 µs within a second.
yos_verify_li5_html: If the RX never enters the bootloader, check the BOOT-pad polarity (active low) and the MOSFET switching with the voltmeter test above.
yos_verify_done_markdown: Once flashed, the same receiver flies — no FTDI left behind.
yos_rp2040_markdown: Prefer the **Waveshare RP2040-Tiny** (~5 USD) — or its twin, the RP2040-Zero, which shares the exact same pinout. All six stances run on the RP2040 with **no readable button at all**: the adapter's BOOT/RESET taps only drive BOOTSEL/RUN, so YOSHIMITSU-RP2040 is driven over the USB serial port, plus a buttonless RESET-tap counter.
yos_rp2040_li1_html: `FLEA` — drop the receiver into its ROM bootloader (MOSFET power-cycle dance), then bridge USB ↔ UART for esptool.
yos_rp2040_li3_html: `POSE <n>` — jump to a stance by number.
yos_rp2040_li4_html: `STATUS` — print the active pin map and the self-test report.
yos_rp2040_li6_html: Quick RESET taps (within ~2 s, counted in flash-backed EEPROM against the AON RTC) advance the stance: 1 = MANJI → 2 = NSS → 3 = BACK → 4 = MEDITATION → 5 = KINCHO.
yos_rp2040_flash_markdown: To flash the RP2040-Tiny itself, hold `BOOT` while power-cycling (it mounts as a mass-storage drive), drop the `.uf2` on it, then press `RESET` once — the board reboots into KINCHO running the new firmware. Configure once, flash once, never touch again.
yos_rp2040_pinmap_markdown: The complete pin map is an editable block at the top of `sketches/yoshimitsu/yoshimitsu.ino` — pin ranges and collisions are validated by a boot POST, and invalid UART numbers refuse to build rather than misbehaving in the air.
yos_h2_library: The library dongle — update without re-touching config
yos_yoshi_markdown: **YOSHI** ("the aurora") is the cheatcode that is *always on*. `YOSHI_RGB` turns the single onboard WS2812B into a living mood-ring: every stance breathes its own colour and rhythm, so you can read the ronin's mind across the room without a single serial byte. Colour *and* blink pattern tell the story — no extra command is needed; the stance *is* the cheatcode, the light is its echo.
yos_aurora_kincho_html: slow green breathing + a crisp double-parry flash (the CRC strike)
yos_aurora_manji_html: a colour wheel spinning like the gyro rotors (the levitation)
yos_aurora_meditation_html: near-dark violet + one slow heartbeat — ready to be flashed
yos_aurora_nss_html: sharp triple-tap flash in blue (blade sheathed, tempo up)
yos_aurora_back_html: near black + one unpredictable crimson glint (the mirror — never looks back)
yos_rgb_markdown: RGB lives on the RP2040-Tiny (`RGB_LED_PIN=16`) behind `YOSHI_RGB`; the ESP32-S3 keeps its sober status LED. Every colour is pure integer math — no `float`, no `malloc`, no `delay()` — and `pumpRgb()` is throttled to ~50 fps so the byte-exact flasher bridge is never disturbed. The hermetic rule holds: the pose switches, the light follows.
yos_jiguang_triangle_markdown: Three names, one soul — this is the cheatcode triangle of the complete solution: **YOSHIMITSU** is the whole Hermetic Shinobi *firmware*; **YOSHI** is the RGB cheatcode (the always-on stance aurora above); and **JIGUANG** (**極光**, "the aurora") is the meditating *administrator* — the unmoved mover who sits cross-legged on the MEDITATION throne and commands the legend from the USB-serial heaven while the ronin keeps flying. JIGUANG is the overqualified storyteller and debug commentator of the Manji legend: Yoshimitsu's voice is functional and terse; JIGUANG's is the myth. The **極光** sigil is written everywhere — hermetically encrypted behind the compile gate `JIGUANG` (`1` = omnipresent, `0` = not a single **極光** byte compiled in).
yos_jiguang_legend_markdown: Easter egg: type `LEGEND` and the whole legend unrolls as one ASCII scroll — the stances, the cheatcodes, the throne and the sigil that never dies. JIGUANG / `jiguang` / **極光** never dies — not in the code, not in the comments, not in this tutorial.
yos_jiguang_levels_markdown: Wake it with `JIGUANG` and the voice climbs four levels: `0` lamb (silent, though explicit commands still answer), `1` tale (boot and every stance change narrated), `2` scroll (+ the CRSF channel readout), and `3` omni (+ the receiver's ELRS debug bytes passed through verbatim). `MUTE` silences it; `CRSF` prints the 16-channel scroll and `SCORE` unrolls the arcade HIGHSCORE ledger — good CRSF frames, failsafe events, bridge bytes and uptime. JIGUANG never seizes the stance: CRSF, servos and the bridge keep obeying the pose while the legend is told.
yos_jiguang_throne_markdown: In MEDITATION the sponge-head is JIGUANG's throne: Yoshimitsu becomes the administrator and takes commands from the USB-serial heaven (`STATUS`, `CRSF`, `SCORE`, `POSE`, `LEGEND`) — more than just flashing. The pose is multifunctional: it saves energy like the old meditation pause, and the ronin sits ready to be flashed. The instant esptool's SLIP byte calls, it yields to the transparent flasher bridge and stays there until MEDITATION re-enters. With `YOSHI_RGB` at level 3 the storyteller also *wears the aurora*: `jiguang(ms)` paints one slow full-spectrum wheel that weaves every stance colour into a single breath. JIGUANG / `jiguang` / **極光** persist as comment and function alike — the invincible part of Yoshimitsu never dies.
yos_library_markdown: YOSHIMITSU follows the **Gralha Azul strategy**: the whole folder is a library dongle. The sketch `sketches/yoshimitsu/yoshimitsu.ino` is only a thin config shell (pins, flags, the BOARD_CUSTOM block); the entire Hermetic Shinobi lives in `src/Yoshimitsu.h`, and every default lives in `src/Yoshimitsu_Padraos.h` (the padrões). To update the dongle: `git pull` the library folder — or drop in a new release — and your config sketch stays untouched. Install it once as an Arduino library (symlink or copy into the libraries folder), then a firmware update is never a re-wire and never a re-configure.
yos_library_li1_html: `src/Yoshimitsu.h` — the whole core: stances, CRSF, MUSHIN, JIGUANG, the flasher bridge.
yos_library_li2_html: `src/Yoshimitsu_Padraos.h` — every default (pins, timings, gate levels) as `*_PADRAO` values.
yos_library_li4_html: `yoshimitsu.ino` — your config only; override anything by defining it before the include.
